abstract: This paper examines paternalistic preferences in two large-scale experiments with participants from the US general population. Participants decide whether to intervene when a stakeholder is about to make a choice misaligned with the stakeholder’s own preferences. Willingness to intervene depends on which intervention is available: only a minority implements a hard intervention, which restricts the stakeholder’s choice set, while a majority implements a soft intervention that provides information without restricting choice. A substantial share of participants does not defer to the stakeholder’s stated preferences when evaluating welfare. Our framework estimates that about half are welfarists and a third libertarian paternalists.
title: Free to Fail? Paternalistic Preferences in the United States

abstract: Despite hydrogen being central to Europe’s decarbonisation strategy, only a small share of renewable hydrogen projects have reached final investment decision. A key barrier is uncertainty about how future hydrogen markets will be designed and operated, particularly under Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin requirements. This study investigates the extent to which future hydrogen market design can be adapted from existing natural gas markets, and the challenges it must address. The analysis was based on a survey on future hydrogen market design targeting European gas transmission system operators, the stakeholder group responsible for operating the network and implementing the Network Codes. The survey provided an assessment of mechanism transferability and identified challenges for the early development of the hydrogen market. Core market design principles and trading frameworks are broadly transferable from natural gas markets, such as entry-exit systems and virtual trading points. Capacity allocation requires targeted adaptation to improve coupling with electricity markets. Tariffs require adaptation through intertemporal cost allocation, distributing infrastructure costs over time to protect early adopters. Balancing regimes should be revisited to reflect hydrogen’s physical characteristics and different linepack flexibility uses. Key challenges for early hydrogen markets include: temporal mismatches between variable renewable supply and expected relatively stable industrial demand, limited operational flexibility due to scarce storage and reduced pipeline linepack, fragmented regional hydrogen clusters, and regulatory uncertainty affecting long-term investment decisions. These findings provide empirical input to the hydrogen Network Codes and offer guidance to policymakers designing hydrogen market frameworks.
title: Towards European hydrogen market design: Perspectives from transmission system operators

abstract: Demand response is a critical component of future energy systems, as it provides a significant contribution to the cost-optimal integration of renewable energy. However, a variety of barriers inhibit its deployment and utilisation. While the research on barriers to demand response is wide and varied, it is often unsystematic and incomplete, with studies focusing on parts of the demand response ecosystem such as specific sectors, technologies or stakeholders. To bridge this gap, this study builds upon existing literature to develop a consistent and comprehensive framework for systematically identifying, classifying and analysing barriers across the demand response ecosystem, with the aim of providing input for the design of policy incentives. We develop an integrated framework that is based on the underlying nature of the identified barriers. We identify four overarching categories: technical, economic, regulatory and behavioural, along with multiple sub-categories and elements. This framework is tested on the Dutch energy system. We find that the most significant technical barriers faced by the Dutch energy sector are process and operational constraints and network limitations; the main economic barriers are financial uncertainty and distorted market signals due to taxes and tariffs; the main regulatory barriers are policy ambiguity and information insufficiency; and the main behavioural barriers are lack of expertise and incompatible individual preferences.
title: Understanding demand-side flexibility characterisation and barriers to effective deployment: A Dutch case study

abstract: Land fragmentation and the resulting constraints on farm management represent a persistent challenge in many rural areas of Poland and Europe. The aim of this paper is to critically examine the effectiveness of land consolidation projects implemented in connection with the construction of the A4 motorway in southern Poland. The analysis covers selected areas where consolidation processes were restricted exclusively to parts of villages located directly adjacent to the linear infrastructure. The assessment was based on classical fragmentation and parcel shape indices as well as basic agrarian structure parameters. The findings clearly indicate that such a narrowly defined scope of interventions yields unsatisfactory outcomes: improvements in land structure are minor, while problems of fragmentation remain essentially unresolved at the village scale. This suggests that the current institutional model, which reduces land consolidation to a compensatory measure limited to motorway surroundings, does not adequately address the real needs of rural areas.
title: Land consolidation in the context of linear infrastructure projects: Adverse outcomes from southern Poland

abstract: In China, a persistent phenomenon known as the “grain-wealth inversion” has been observed, characterized by “grain-producing counties with poor economies”. At its core, this represents an institutional misallocation of opportunity costs under the farmland protection system, manifesting as “localized costs and socialized benefits”. This phenomenon is fundamentally distinct from the curse associated with mineral resource dependency. Given the prevalent deficiencies in existing research, including imprecise causal identification, unverified chain transmission mechanisms, a lack of refined quantitative tools, and the absence of precise governance strategies, this study utilized multi-source raster data from five periods spanning 2000–2020. It integrated econometric causal inference with GIS spatial analysis techniques to conduct a systematic, multi-scale research across “provincial-city-county-grid” levels. This study constructed a Farmland Resource Curse Index (FRCI), validated transmission mechanism through a cross-verification approach employing causal mediation effects and path analysis, thereby establishing a multi-level causal evidence chain encompassing “statistical correlation — single-path identification — multi-path verification — instrumental-variable corroboration”. The primary findings were as follows: 1) China was subject to the farmland resource curse (FRC), with the instrumental variable method confirming the direction and magnitude of the benchmark regression. 2) The FRCI represented a spatial distribution with generally higher values in the north and lower values in the southeast, showing a gradual overall increase over the past two decades and a northeastward migration in its center of gravity by 213.63 km, with the most notable intensification of the curse observed in major grain-producing areas. 3) Abundant farmland resource endowments (FREs) impeded economic growth through six parallel pathways and five chain pathways, with the total chain effect contributing to 48.89% of the overall impact, thereby confirming the transmission framework of “FREs → land use → factor allocation → structural transformation → economic growth”. 4) The uneven distribution of FRE further intensified regional disparities in the curse’s severity, with significant regional heterogeneity evident in effects. Based on these findings, a dual-dimensional precise governance system was proposed, centered on the FRCI and incorporating “zoning regulation and control + hierarchical governance”, to provide a scientific foundation for balancing national food security with regional coordinated development.

abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .

abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .

abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .

title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions

abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. abstract: This paper examines the impact of artificial intelligence on within-firm wage inequality using panel data on Chinese A-share listed companies over the period 2007–2023. The analysis shows that the adoption of artificial intelligence significantly narrows wage disparities, primarily by reshaping labor demand—reducing reliance on low-skilled workers while increasing both demand and wages for high-skilled employees. The effect is stronger in non-state-owned firms, firms with greater CEO power, those facing fewer financing constraints, high-tech industries, and regions with higher levels of marketization. By providing firm-level evidence on how artificial intelligence influences compensation structures, the paper contributes to the literature on technology and labor markets, with implications for corporate governance and policies aimed at promoting more inclusive growth.

abstract: The bulk of cash is held for store of value purposes, with such holdings increasing in times of high economic uncertainty and only a share of the population choosing to hoard cash. We develop a Diamond and Dybvig model with cash & reserves and heterogeneous beliefs about the state of the economy that accounts for this evidence. Only consumers who are sufficiently pessimistic hold cash as a store of value. When economic uncertainty increases, consumers and banks rebalance their portfolios towards safe assets. The introduction of a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) lowers lending and productive investment by reducing the storage cost of public money. We find that several factors can mitigate this bank disintermediation effect, including banks’ optimal response (increased relative maturity transformation), deposit insurance, a cash-like CBDC and certain state-contingent CBDC design features. CBDC has heterogeneous welfare consequences across the population. We characterize conditions under which CBDC improves social welfare.
title: Public money as a store of value, heterogeneous beliefs and banks: Implications of CBDC

abstract: Discrimination in the labour market could affect mental health. Using age-based discontinuities that affect employment eligibility in China, this study evaluates the effects of age discrimination in the labour market. We find that individuals just above the eligibility threshold of age 35 are less likely to be employed than those just below the threshold but do not experience significantly higher risk of depression. Neither are they more likely to change health behaviours (e.g. drinking, smoking or exercising). Exploration of mechanisms suggests that individuals are more likely to turn to religion for relief. Religiosity can potentially attenuate the detrimental effect of discrimination on mental health.

abstract: Research on input trade liberalization and firm innovation has yielded mixed conclusions. This paper asks whether capital goods trade liberalization constitutes a distinct channel that promotes innovation. Exploiting China's 2001 WTO accession, which sharply reduced tariffs on capital goods, and cross-industry variation in pre-WTO tariff rates, we show that manufacturing firms in industries facing larger cuts experienced significantly greater post-WTO innovation. Specifically, a one-percentage-point higher pre-WTO capital goods tariff raises the post-WTO probability that a firm files at least one patent by 1.36 percentage points (41% of the pre-WTO mean of 3.35%) and increases average patent filings by 3.2% of the pre-WTO mean. Our results are consistent with firms gaining greater access to imported, technology-embodied capital goods, which complemented in-house R&D and spurred adaptive innovation, as reflected in a disproportionate rise in utility-model patents.

abstract: We show that exporting reshapes the migrant-native wage gap. We develop a model with heterogeneous firms and directed search, showing that high-skilled immigrants lower fixed export costs by leveraging destination-specific knowledge. The model generates an information premium for these workers in exporting firms that can offset immigrant-specific labour-market disadvantages. Using Portuguese employer-employee data linked to customs records, we observe a closing of the migrant-native wage gap among high-skilled workers in exporting firms, so that high-skilled immigrants earn wages comparable to those of high-skilled natives. We find no such results for low-skilled workers. To test the information premium hypothesis, we exploit differences across immigrants’ origin countries and firms’ export destinations. Our results indicate that destination-specific exporting can help reduce the wage gap, especially for high-skilled occupations. We thus provide micro-level evidence that immigrants’ export-facilitating role translates into wage premia within firms.
title: When immigrants meet exporters: A reassessment of the migrant-native wage gap

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the international spillovers of China’s fiscal policy and identify the financial channel as a pivotal transmission mechanism. Using monthly data from 2001 to 2019 and a sign-restricted Bayesian SVAR model, we document three stylized facts: First, China’s fiscal expansion crowds in domestic consumption and investment while inducing a mild trade deficit. Second, it triggers a persistent real appreciation of the Renminbi, despite systematic monetary accommodation. Third, it generates positive spillovers to the global economy, boosting commodity prices, output, and asset prices. These findings are robust when the global risky-asset factor is replaced with alternative measures of global bank balance-sheet activity. To rationalize these patterns, we develop a two-country New Keynesian model featuring financially constrained global intermediaries. We demonstrate that a balance-sheet channel underpins these positive spillovers: fiscal expansion, supported by accommodative monetary policy, improves global intermediaries’ net worth, relaxes their leverage constraints, and lowers credit spreads, culminating in a “prosper-thy-neighbor” expansion. This mechanism acts as an international financial accelerator, amplifying the domestic stimulus, yielding a fiscal multiplier above one and generating a sizable foreign spillover multiplier. Counterfactual analysis shows that removing this financial channel reverts the economy to a “beggar-thy-neighbor” outcome where foreign output declines. Furthermore, we show that in a monetary union, these positive spillovers are amplified when the common central bank accommodates the fiscal expansion, leading to larger stimulus effects for both countries.

abstract: This note provides simple rules and formulas for deriving closed form confidence sets by inverting the Anderson-Rubin (AR) test in the important case of one endogenous covariate and one instrument. I demonstrate that these confidence sets can be easily constructed using standard output from three regressions: the first stage, the reduced form, and a modified reduced form. The procedure is the same for a wide variety of standard error estimators. Furthermore, I provide graphical intuition for the confidence sets that we get from inverting the AR test using instrumental confidence regions within the coordinate system of the first stage and reduced form slope coefficients.
title: Simple closed form Anderson-Rubin confidence sets

abstract: The matrix exponential spatial specification (MESS) recovers its dependence parameter when disturbances exhibit large impulses, as occur under Cauchy and log-Cauchy distributions. The zero diagonal of the weight matrix W eliminates the leading contamination term from the gradient, leaving an O ( 1 / n ) bias under standard constructions. Monte Carlo experiments without regression signal show the standard deviation under Cauchy errors is 24% smaller than under t ( 200 ) errors, with robustness across weight matrices and gradual degradation under nuisance regressors and spatial fixed effects.
title: A cauchy MESS

abstract: Can firm-level ambiguity reduce crash risk when short selling is constrained? Ambiguity facilitates bad-news hoarding, raising crash risk, but also discourages ambiguity-averse investors from sustaining overvaluation when pessimistic beliefs cannot be expressed. During China’s market-wide short-sale ban, the ambiguity–crash risk relation is U-shaped among firms with limited analyst coverage but not among better-covered firms, though the cross-group difference is imprecise. The U-shape survives volatility and illiquidity controls and lower-tail trimming. After stocks become eligible for short selling, firms with higher pre-treatment ambiguity show more negative crash-risk responses, with no detectable differential pre-trend. Short-sale constraints and information production are boundary conditions.

abstract: In recent years, an emerging body of empirical research has shown that tax audits, in addition to recovering unpaid taxes (the direct effect), increase future tax compliance (the indirect or dynamic effect). This literature also suggests that the revision of expectations about future audits induced by audit experience plays an important role in explaining this indirect effect. However, how exactly taxpayers form their beliefs and adjust them based on audit experience remains an open question. This paper extends tax evasion theory by introducing a novel framework embedded with a Bayesian audit belief updating mechanism. This allows us to formally model how taxpayers internalize past audit experiences to dynamically adjust their perceived probability of an audit. Applying this model to analyze the dynamic impact of audits on tax evasion behavior, we find that our predictions align with all patterns of the indirect effect observed in the empirical literature: it is positive for non-compliant taxpayers, and it persists but attenuates over time.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
title: Tax audit expectation updating: Direct and indirect effects of an audit

abstract: This paper provides causal evidence on how state-led institutional reform in public forest management affects wildfire risk. We examine a reform in China that restructures state-owned forest farms as nonprofit public institutions, shifting their funding to government budgets and tightening enforcement of logging restrictions. Using a difference-in-differences design based on historical farm-town boundaries, we find that the reform lowers forest-fire incidence by roughly 10%. The effects peak during local political turnover and are stronger in areas upwind of local jurisdictions, suggesting that political incentives and accountability shape implementation. Fire declines are larger among farms located in counties with stronger fiscal capacity, which provide greater subsidies, and among farms with higher compliance with logging restrictions, highlighting public financing and regulatory enforcement as key channels. We also observe modest positive spillovers into adjacent woodlands. Accounting for spillover effects in nearby control areas implies a reduction of over 20% in forest fires within state forest farms. A simple cost-benefit analysis shows that health benefits are the main source of monetized gains and that benefits exceed costs under the spillover-adjusted estimate. Our findings illustrate how state capacity can be mobilized through public financing and regulatory authority to generate tangible environmental and social gains in publicly managed forests.

abstract: We match granular supervisory and credit register data to examine the role of banks’ exposure to interest rate risk in the transmission of monetary policy to bank lending in the euro area. Exploiting the steepest and fastest rate hikes since the inception of the euro, we find that banks with larger net duration gaps - after accounting for hedging - cut corporate lending more and rebalance their portfolios away from longer-term, fixed-rate loans. This occurs as these banks anticipate weaker medium-term profitability and capital growth. Firms borrowing from these banks cannot fully substitute credit to other banks, resulting in a stronger overall contraction in borrowing. This reduction is especially strong for firms that are smaller, more risky, and have less bank relationships.
title: Are low interest rates firing back? Interest rate risk in the banking book and bank lending in a rising interest rate environment

abstract: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict disrupted global energy trade and repriced euro area financial markets. Using a daily event-targeted vector autoregression, we estimate the effects of Hormuz-related geopolitical shocks on equities, sovereign yields, inflation expectations, and core–periphery spreads. A negative shock comparable to the initial closure reduces the Euro Stoxx by over 4%, raises German one-year yields by about 30 basis points and inflation swaps by 15 basis points, and widens spreads. Historical decompositions show these shocks explained much of the initial market response, though other factors became increasingly important as markets adapted.
title: Strait of Hormuz crisis and euro area financial market spillovers: An event-targeted approach

abstract: Meta-analysis is standard in economics, and its reporting guidelines ask for data deposits without saying at what precision. Effect sizes are computed from rounded statistics; coding files record counts formed by rounding estimated shares. Treating them as exact distorts the between-study variance through two channels: an added variance and an effect-dependent systematic shift. It is easily missed: a plug-in within-study variance from the same inputs absorbs part of it. On two dishonesty data sets whose exact counts survive, it absorbs 72 to 88 percent; correcting only the first channel recovers about seventy percent, and on a plug-in variance it overshoots.
title: Rounding in data deposits distorts meta-analytic heterogeneity

abstract: We experimentally examine firms’ incentives to provide information that enables consumers to learn about product valuations. In our design, firms make take-it-or-leave-it offers to consumers who are uncertain about their own valuations. Firms can choose to facilitate learning without observing what consumers learn. Consistent with theory, firms are more likely to provide information when ex-ante gains from trade are low, particularly when marginal costs are high. Consumers, however, depart from the benchmark model: acceptance rates are lower when the absence of learning is chosen by the firm than when exogenously imposed, even though the firm’s choice conveys no information about valuation. Firms that permit learning charge higher prices, but, relative to theory, low-cost firms oversupply information while high-cost firms undersupply it. These patterns are consistent with consumer responses to intentional nondisclosure influencing firms’ pricing and information provision.
title: When should firms promote consumer learning? An experimental study

abstract: The equity lending and option market both allow investors to decouple voting and cash flow rights of common shares. We provide a theory of this decoupling. While either market enables investors to acquire voting rights without cash flow exposure, empirical studies demonstrate a substantial difference in implied vote prices. Our model explains this surprising difference by uncovering the mechanism by which vote prices in the equity lending market are endogenously lower than those implied by the option market. We show that even though votes are cheaper in the equity lending market, activists endogenously choose to purchase votes in both markets.
title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights

abstract: Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.
title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results

abstract: This paper studies the impact of offshoring by US firms on voting patterns in the US. Using county-level voting data combined with industry-level offshoring data, we ask whether an increase in employment at foreign affiliates of US multinationals in vertically oriented industries is associated with an increase in the vote share for the incumbent party candidate in Presidential, House, and Senate elections. We find that offshoring leads to an increase in the incumbent vote share for counties with more educated workers, and a decrease for counties with higher shares of workers in the manufacturing sector and in occupations that are more easily relocated abroad. These results are consistent with the labor market literature on offshoring, which shows that offshoring has heterogeneous effects on workers’ employment based on skill and occupational tasks. This suggests that voters respond to the economic effects of offshoring by rewarding or punishing incumbent party candidates.
title: Offshoring and voting patterns in the US

abstract: In many countries, minimum wage policies allow employers to pay young workers less than adults, and the UK is now debating how fast to phase out its lower youth minima. But do employers actually use the room that age-specific minimum wages give them? This column uses the introduction of the UK National Living Wage, which raised the minimum wage only for workers aged 25 and over, to show that employers in a low-wage sector also raised the pay of younger colleagues. These spillovers happen inside firms, within job roles, and seem to be driven by pay equity norms.
title: Company wage policy in a low-wage labour market

abstract: Europe’s push for deeper capital markets assumes that cross-border equity ownership matters. This column shows that it does. Euro area listed firms remain heavily owned by domestic investors. When COVID-19 struck, firms in the hardest-hit sectors with more domestically concentrated shareholders cut investment more, lost more value, and raised less equity than peers with diversified shareholder bases. Capital markets union is hence not just about financial integration. It is about real economic resilience.
authors: Elena Banu, Lea Best, Francesca Vinci

abstract: This paper shows that firms value liability maturity opacity when selecting funding sources in their debt structure. Such opacity may protect proprietary information about project timelines and enable strategic management of disclosures to lenders. Exploiting FASB ASC 842's mandatory lease maturity disclosure requirements as a plausibly exogenous shock, I document how losing maturity opacity affects firms' financing decisions. Isolating the maturity opacity channel from balance sheet recognition effects, I find that following the policy announcement, firms with higher pre-policy maturity opacity significantly reduce their lease usage by 0.9 percentage points (36% of the sample mean). The reduction concentrates in long-term leases, which were previously the most opaque in maturity structure. They also decrease their reliance on bank credit lines, consistent with avoiding heightened scrutiny from better-informed creditors. Consistent with the economic model of leases in Eisfeldt and Rampini (2009), these firms increase secured debt usage by 7.5 percentage points (19.7% of the sample mean) after implementation of the policy. These effects are stronger among firms with low analyst coverage, among financially constrained firms, and in competitive industries, where maturity opacity is more valuable. The findings document firms' preference for liability maturity opacity and reveal a new mechanism through which lease accounting reform shapes debt structure.
title: Liability maturity opacity and debt structure: Evidence from lease accounting reform

abstract: We study information design in strategic settings when agents can publicly refuse to view their private signals. Ignoring the constraints that agents must be willing to view their signals may lead to substantial divergence between the designer’s intent and actual outcomes, even in the case where the designer seeks to maximize the agents’ payoffs. We introduce the appropriate equilibrium concept — ignorance-permissive Bayes correlated equilibrium — and characterize implementable distributions over states and actions. The designer’s optimal response to strategic ignorance generates qualitative properties that standard information design cannot: the designer may provide redundant or even counterproductive information, asymmetric information structures may be strictly optimal in symmetric environments, providing information conditional on players’ viewing choices rather than all at once may hurt the designer, and communication between players may help her. Optimality sometimes requires that players ignore their signals with positive probability.
title: Strategic Ignorance and Information Design

abstract: I study security design with moral hazard and two-sided limited liability when an entrepreneur can choose any distribution of project returns subject to a cost. I first characterize which return distributions can be induced by a security and when the first-best can be financed. Whenever the first-best can be financed, it is optimal and can be implemented by debt; more generally, any security that implements it pays the investor a constant amount on the support of the first-best distribution. The agency costs that may prevent first-best financing are related to the convexity of the cost function. For a given return distribution, greater convexity of the cost function increases the rent that the entrepreneur has to retain and can therefore make first-best financing more difficult. When the first-best cannot be financed, I derive second-best distributions for cost functions that are monotone in risk or depend on generalized moments. Under suitable conditions, the second-best is first-order stochastically dominated by the first-best. The optimal return distributions I characterize have finite support. Since an optimal security is uniquely determined only on, but not off, the support of the optimal return distribution, optimal securities are not unique.
title: Security design with flexible moral hazard and limited liability
